subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Chai: India's National Drink Wasn't Always Popular
description: A quick, practical guide to Chai: India's National Drink Wasn't Always Popular.

hook.text: India is the world's biggest tea-drinking nation—but most Indians barely drank tea before the 1900s.

buildup.text: The British grew tea in India for export. Domestic consumption was tiny. Indians preferred water, milk, and local beverages.

discovery.text: The Indian Tea Association launched aggressive marketing in the 1900s—free samples at train stations and factories.

twist.text: Indians rejected plain British-style tea. They added milk, sugar, and spices—creating masala chai, a completely reinvented drink.

climax.text: By independence in 1947, chai was India's national drink. An imported colonial commodity had been domesticated and remade.

punchline.text: Britain pushed tea on India. India turned it into something entirely its own.

quiz.question: How did Indians change British-style tea into masala chai?
options: They added milk, sugar, and spices—completely reinventing the drink

details.summary: Tea was virtually unknown in India until the British promoted it in the early 20th century to create a domestic market. The distinctively spiced masala chai that India is now famous for was invented by street vendors who added milk, sugar, and spices to stretch expensive tea leaves further.
details.whyItMatters: India's transformation from a tea-indifferent nation to the world's largest tea-consuming country happened within living memory, showing how quickly beverage culture can change.
takeaways: British tea companies promoted tea in India to build a new market
Street vendors created masala chai to stretch expensive tea leaves
India went from no tea culture to the largest consumer in decades

faq.question: What spices are traditionally used in masala chai?
faq.answer: Classic masala chai includes cardamom, cinnamon, ginger, cloves, and black pepper, though recipes vary by region and family. The spices are simmered with black tea, milk, and sugar to create a richly aromatic, sweet, and warming drink.

faq.question: How did the British Tea Association promote tea consumption in India?
faq.answer: They deployed tea boys at factories and train stations to offer free or cheap tea to workers. They also used advertising and created tea breaks in industrial settings, gradually building a habit that became a deeply rooted national tradition.
